Content:
The intermediate value theorem (IVT) states that:

Content:
> If [MATH: f(x)] is continuous on [MATH: \color{blue}[a,b],] and [MATH: k] is a number between [MATH: \color{red}{f(a)}] and [MATH: \color{red}{f(b)}] inclusively, then there exists a number [MATH: c \in \color{blue}{[a,b]}] such that [MATH: f(c)=k.]

Content:
The intuition behind the IVT is that if a function is continuous between two inputs, then between those two inputs, we must be able to draw the function without picking up our pen off the page, so the function must cover all values between the two corresponding outputs.

Content:

  • On the subinterval [MATH: [{\color{blue}0},{\color{blue}1}],] we have [MATH: g({\color{blue}0})={\color{red}-3}] and [MATH: g({\color{blue}1})={\color{red}5}.] Since [MATH: -2 \in [{\color{red}-3},{\color{red}5}],] the IVT does guarantee a solution to the equation [MATH: g(x)=-2] on this subinterval.

  • On the subinterval [MATH: [{\color{blue}1},{\color{blue}2}],] we have [MATH: g({\color{blue}1})={\color{red}5}] and [MATH: g({\color{blue}2})={\color{red}3}.] Since [MATH: -2 \not \in[{\color{red}3},{\color{red}5}],] the IVT does not guarantee a solution to the equation [MATH: g(x)=-2] on this subinterval.

The IVT guarantees solutions to [MATH: g(x)=-2] on the subintervals [MATH: [-1,0]] and [MATH: [0,1].] Therefore, [MATH: g(x)=-2] has at least two solutions.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The intermediate value theorem (IVT) states that:

Content:
> If [MATH: f(x)] is continuous on [MATH: \color{blue}[a,b],] and [MATH: k] is a number between [MATH: \color{red}{f(a)}] and [MATH: \color{red}{f(b)}] inclusively, then there exists a number [MATH: c \in \color{blue}{[a,b]}] such that [MATH: f(c)=k.]

Content:
The intuition behind the IVT is that if a function is continuous between two inputs, then between those two inputs, we must be able to draw the function without picking up our pen off the page, so the function must cover all values between the two corresponding outputs.

Content:
The IVT is often used to prove that some equation has a solution. For example, if we want to prove that there is a solution to [MATH: f(x)=3,] and we know that [MATH: f(x)] is a continuous function with [MATH: f({\color{blue}{1}})={\color{red}{2}}] and [MATH: f({\color{blue}{6}})={\color{red}{6}},] then the IVT tells us that there exists some solution [MATH: c \in \color{blue}{[1,6]}] such that [MATH: f(c)=3.]

Content:
We can gain further intuition by visualizing the situation. First, let's plot what [MATH: y=f(x)] might look like.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/37cd1acc19a6c3f1ec28de339987035d]

Content:
For this particular [MATH: f(x)] there is one solution to [MATH: f(x)=3], which is [MATH: x\approx 2.] Note that our solution lies inside the interval [MATH: \color{blue}[1,6].]

Content:
Now let's consider another possible [MATH: f(x).]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/57f39e1bfa7c0834cbbcead1d0b6626b]

Content:
This time, there are three solutions to [MATH: f(x)=3] which lie in the interval [MATH: \color{blue}[1,6].]

Content:
We can keep changing our [MATH: f(x),] but no matter how we draw it, we will always have some solution to [MATH: f(x)=3] which lies in the interval [MATH: \color{blue}[1,6].]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/a71554c73083dc0559d0f1ee69158ad3]

---

Item 2 — Example: Completing a Statement On the Intermediate Value Theorem

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/6e256c36411942eac5fc5523f999c4c3]

The function [MATH: y=f(x)] above is defined and continuous on the closed interval [MATH: x\in [-5,2].] By filling the blank spaces in the sentence below, complete the statement of the intermediate value theorem:

> If [MATH: k] is a number that lies between [MATH: \textrm{ ________ }] inclusively, then there exists a number [MATH: c \in [-5,2]] such that [MATH: f(c)=k.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The function [MATH: f(x)] is continuous on [MATH: [-5,2],] so the intermediate value theorem guarantees that [MATH: f(x)=k] has a solution for each value of [MATH: k] between [MATH: f(-5)] and [MATH: f(2).]

Since [MATH: f(-5)=1] and [MATH: f(2)=4], we must have [MATH: k\in[1,4].]

Therefore, the missing part is "[MATH: 1] and [MATH: 4]". The complete sentence is:

> If [MATH: k] is a number that lies between [MATH: 1] and [MATH: 4] inclusively, then there exists a number [MATH: c \in [-5,2]] such that [MATH: f(c)=k.]

Since [MATH: g] is a continuous function on [MATH: [-2,2]], we can apply the intermediate value theorem (IVT) in any subinterval of [MATH: [-2,2].]

So, we will go through each subinterval of [MATH: [-2,2]] and check if the IVT guarantees a solution to the equation [MATH: g(x)=-2] on this interval.

- On the subinterval [MATH: [{\color{blue}-2},{\color{blue}-1}],] we have [MATH: g({\color{blue}-2})={\color{red}4}] and [MATH: g({\color{blue}-1})={\color{red}-1}.] Since [MATH: -2 \not \in [{\color{red}-1},{\color{red}4}],] the IVT does not guarantee a solution to the equation [MATH: g(x)=-2] on this subinterval.
- On the subinterval [MATH: [{\color{blue}-1},{\color{blue}0}],] we have [MATH: g({\color{blue}-1})={\color{red}-1}] and [MATH: g({\color{blue}0})={\color{red}-3}.] Since [MATH: -2 \in [{\color{red}-3},{\color{red}-1}],] the IVT does guarantee a solution to the equation [MATH: g(x)=-2] on this subinterval.
- On the subinterval [MATH: [{\color{blue}0},{\color{blue}1}],] we have [MATH: g({\color{blue}0})={\color{red}-3}] and [MATH: g({\color{blue}1})={\color{red}5}.] Since [MATH: -2 \in [{\color{red}-3},{\color{red}5}],] the IVT does guarantee a solution to the equation [MATH: g(x)=-2] on this subinterval.
- On the subinterval [MATH: [{\color{blue}1},{\color{blue}2}],] we have [MATH: g({\color{blue}1})={\color{red}5}] and [MATH: g({\color{blue}2})={\color{red}3}.] Since [MATH: -2 \not \in[{\color{red}3},{\color{red}5}],] the IVT does not guarantee a solution to the equation [MATH: g(x)=-2] on this subinterval.

The IVT guarantees solutions to [MATH: g(x)=-2] on the subintervals [MATH: [-1,0]] and [MATH: [0,1].] Therefore, [MATH: g(x)=-2] has at least two solutions.
